The Coast Guard inspector arrived on Tuesday morning with a clipboard and an anonymous complaint.

He was a young petty officer named Haskins, embarrassed and thorough, and he spent three hours crawling through the *Margaret Ann* with a flashlight while Wren stood on the pier and turned away the eight o'clock passengers one by one. At eleven he climbed out of the engine compartment with grease on his cheek and an expression of real regret.

"Cracked exhaust manifold," he said. "Port side. You've got carbon monoxide getting into the passenger cabin when she's under load. It's not much, but it's not nothing, and with kids aboard..." He wrote on the clipboard. "I have to ground her, ma'am. Until it's replaced and re-inspected."

"How long?"

"That's up to your mechanic."

Her mechanic was Dell Ruiz at the boatyard, who came down at noon, looked at the manifold for ninety seconds, and swore in two languages.

"It's a Detroit 6-71 from 1968," Dell said. "Nobody makes this manifold. I can call around. Maybe there's one in a yard in Nova Scotia, maybe there's one on a dead boat in New Jersey. Maybe two weeks. Maybe never."

"I have seven days."

"Then I'll call fast." He wiped his hands. "Wren, who complained? That crack's been there a year at least. Your dad knew about it. Anybody who's ridden this boat in the back row knows the cabin smells like a bus station."

Wren didn't answer. She didn't have to. She thought of a camel overcoat, a man who looked at boats instead of water.

She found Tobias at the end of the pier afterward, sitting with his legs over the edge where they used to fish as kids. She sat down next to him. For a long time, neither of them said anything. The tide was going out. The pilings stood bare and black and dripping, crusted with barnacles their grandfather had never seen.

"I keep thinking about the August night he drowned," she said finally. "How the water must have felt. Whether he knew."

Tobias was quiet. Then: "I took money from him."

She turned.

"Ten years ago. That's what the fight was about." He was looking at the water, not at her. "I was nineteen and stupid and I owed some people in Portland for a card game I should never have sat down at. Four thousand dollars. I took it out of the ferry account. I thought I'd pay it back before he noticed. He noticed in about a day." He laughed without any humor at all. "He didn't care about the money. He said so. He cared that I didn't ask. He said, *You could have asked me for anything, and you took it instead.* And I said some things. And he threw my bag off the pier."

"Toby."

"I never paid it back. I meant to. Every year I meant to." He finally looked at her, and his eyes were red. "That's why I didn't come to the funeral. I couldn't stand there in front of the whole town owing him. It's stupid. I know it's stupid."

Wren thought of the ledger. Forty years of her father's small upright hand. She thought of Ada saying, *It never tells you what was owed.*

"He wrote it down," she said slowly. "Didn't he. Somewhere. Four thousand dollars, Tobias Halloway."

"Knowing him? Probably with interest."

She wanted to put her arm around him. She did not know how anymore. She put her hand flat on the weathered boards between them instead, close to his, and he looked at it, and after a while he put his hand next to hers, not touching, and they sat like that until the tide turned.
